hints: Focus on what changes and what stays the same when many ethene molecules join to make polyethene.
Remember ethene is an alkene with a C=C double bond, while polyethene is a long saturated alkane chain.
Think about which reagent oxidises a C=C bond in the cold, and why that test fails once the double bond is gone.
walkthrough:
**Write out monomer and polymer**

Think of ethene as $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2$ and polyethene as $\text{-(CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-)}_n$. Polymerisation just opens the double bond to join units together.

Addition polymerisation:
$$n\text{C}_2\text{H}_4 \rightarrow \text{-(CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-)}_n$$

**Compare empirical formulae**

Both monomer $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ and the repeat unit $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ simplify to the same empirical formula, $\text{CH}_2$. So nothing is lost, only joined.

**Compare reactivity toward oxidation**

The key difference is the functional group. Ethene has a reactive C=C bond that is easily oxidised in the cold by aqueous bromine or cold dilute $\text{MnO}_4^-$. Polyethene has only single C-C and C-H bonds, like an alkane, so it resists cold oxidation and needs strong heat to burn.

Cold test for alkene:
$$\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 + [O] + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{cold, dilute MnO}_4^-} \text{CH}_2\text{OH-CH}_2\text{OH}$$

**Check fuels and intermolecular forces**

Both will burn with heat to give $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so both can act as fuels. And the huge polymer chain has far more contact points, so it has much stronger van der Waals forces than tiny ethene molecules.

options.A: Incorrect. Addition polymerisation does not change atom ratio. Ethene, $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$, has empirical formula $\text{CH}_2$ and polyethene, $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_4)_n$, also has empirical formula $\text{CH}_2$.
options.B: Correct. Ethene is unsaturated and decolourises cold dilute $\text{MnO}_4^-$ or bromine water without heating. Polyethene is saturated with only sigma bonds, so it cannot be oxidised in the cold in this way.
options.C: Incorrect. Both burn exothermically in oxygen. Ethene burns as a gas fuel, and polyethene (like other plastics) also burns when heated strongly, giving $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
options.D: Incorrect, it is the opposite. Van der Waals forces increase with chain length and surface contact. The very long polymer chains have far greater induced dipole attractions than small $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ molecules, which is why ethene is a gas and polyethene is a solid.
